thread.title: Dow Gains 114 Points as Trade Worries Fade

author: Teresa Rivas
title: Dow Gains 114 Points as Trade Worries Fade
text:
Illustration: Getty Images By Teresa Rivas Sept. 11, 2018 5:05 p.m. ET Turn That Frown Upside Down . Morning weakness on trade was quickly forgotten by Tuesday afternoon , helped by optimism from small businesses. Then there’s the excitement about the upcoming Apple (AAPL) event. In today’s After the Bell we…
• Examine why U.S. stocks have held up, and; • Why international markets haven’t been as lucky; • Highlight Activision Blizzard’s winning session. Second Verse Same as the First
You can’t keep a good market down: Early worries about trade quickly faded from investors’ minds this afternoon, as things in the U.S. appear to remain solid, even if overseas markets weren’t so lucky .
The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 113.99 points, or 0.44%, to 25,971.06, while the S&P 500 rose 10.76 points, or 0.37%, to 2887.89, and the Nasdaq Composite climbed 48.31 points, or 0.61%, to 7972.47.
Newsletter Sign-up By contrast, European stocks ended lower, and Hong Kong’s Hang Seng fell into bear market territory . It’s the same story we’ve seen over and over again this summer: The strong U.S. economy has kept domestic investors looking on the bright side, with international markets bearing the brunt of the pain.
There’s a good rationale for that, says Leumi Investment Services’ Humberto Garcia . Strong corporate earnings and indications that fiscal and monetary policy will remain largely accommodative underpin optimism about U.S. markets, making emerging-market pain less unlikely to upend domestic stocks. “Contagion by any other name would sting just as sharply,” he writes. “Yet the virulence of isolated financial troubles among a handful of EM countries appears to be contained by stronger global financial institutions, a functioning early warning system, and willingness to permit quicker multilateral and bilateral interventions.”
So as long as the U.S. economy continues to show strength, investors seem willing to brush off trade worries, even as more tariffs loom.
In fact, for September, a month that’s historically been unkind to markets, we’ve actually gotten off pretty easy thus far. Sure, the Cboe Volatility Index, or the VIX, is higher, but TD Ameritrade’s JJ Kinahan writes that market choppiness shouldn’t be a surprise right now. “Investors are continuing to digest geopolitical issues and read the tea leaves on the Federal Reserve’s interest rate expectations even as the U.S. market and economy seem to be chugging along.”
It’s not only the economy helping the bulls run, though. As DataTrek’s Nicholas Colas notes, there are more positive indicators from credit markets that support stocks’ climbing further, including easing worries on Eurozone debt, to a lower Treasury Eurodollar spread, and plenty of appetite for corporate bonds. Reason enough, he writes, to remain bullish.
Party on, Wayne.
The Hot Stock
Activision Blizzard (ATVI) shot to the top of the S&P 500 Tuesday, helped by positive gamer feedback and a vote of confidence from Stifel .
Activision Blizzard rose $5.24, or 7.1%, to $79.50.
Gamers are happy with the company’s latest Call of Duty, due out next month, with some saying it could knock down a peg or two the newly popular Fortnite. In addition, Stifel’s Drew Crum reiterated a Buy rating and $82 price target on the stock today, moving it to his firm’s Select List (while removing Electronic Arts (EA)), in part citing his analysis of pre-sales for some of Activision’s key game titles.
Activision is up 25.6% year to date, and has gained 20.1% in the past 12 months.
The top five stocks in the S&P 500:
Activision Blizzard: 7.1%
United Rentals (URI): 5.3%
Take-Two Interactive Software (TTWO): 3.7%
CenturyLink (CTL): 3.2%
Concho Resources (CXO): 3%
The Biggest Loser
AmerisourceBergen (ABC) sank to the bottom of the index, following news of the resignation of its chief financial officer.
AmerisourceBergen lost $4.23, or 4.8%, to $84.10.
After the close of trading Monday, the company said CFO Tim Guttman would retire from the company, effective Nov. 9, and will be replaced by James Clearly , who currently serves as the group president of Global Commercialization Services and Animal Health.
Barclays’ Steve Valiquette called the move a “modest surprise,” and reiterated an Equal Weight rating on AmerisourceBergen. “[I]t is unclear if this CFO change will impact investor psychology in relation to a potential full acquisition of AmerisourceBergen by Walgreens Boots Alliance (WBA) for the remaining 74% it does not currently own.”
AmerisourceBergen is down 8.4% year to date, and has lost 0.3% in the past 12 months.
The bottom five stocks in the S&P 500:
AmerisourceBergen: -4.8%
Western Digital (WDC): -3.6%
Broadcom (AVGO): - 3.4%
Nektar Therapeutics (NKTR): -3.3%
Intel (INTC): -3%
